<reason>CON built a coherent case around command, continuity, and "dual unavailability," and its pressure questions forced PRO to concede a small permanent command core. But PRO had pre-emptively set aside that core in its opening, so the concession cost little, and PRO consistently framed the motion as where the country's center of gravity sits. The decisive turn came when CON's own A2 answer sourced the surge hands from "contractors, allies, and assisting specialists" — PRO's closing seized this to show both sides now agree civilians do the defense in the crisis hour, leaving only the question of whether they are organized and cleared in advance. CON's rejoinder ("help is not reliance") is a real distinction but largely restates earlier lines rather than explaining why unorganized contractors beat a pre-cleared reserve. PRO also gave a substantive mechanism answer to dual unavailability (cleared reservist receives indicators, pre-agreed release status, non-target responders surge in) that CON answered only by repetition. PRO's clipped rebuttal and slight looseness on the Estonia 2007/CDL timeline are minor costs; PRO still narrowed and resolved the clash more effectively.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>PRO's closing capture of CON's A4.2 concession — that surge hands in a NotPetya hour come from contractors and specialists — reframing the whole dispute as "cyber-reserve" versus "cyber-reserve without the preparation." CON's "help is not reliance" reply did not neutralize it.</best_rebuttal>
